feedback: If a child answers 'fish' for the dolphin because of fins or swimming, re-run the three mammal tests — breathes air, feeds milk, keeps its body warm — which it passes.
If a child answers 'mammal' for the shark, point to its gills and the fact that it does not feed its babies milk: those features make it a fish.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can independently justify the category with defining features and apply the test to an animal they were not taught directly.
learnerActions: Sort a fresh set of animals into mammal vs fish.
Answer 'Why is a dolphin a mammal?' choosing the feature-based reason (breathes air / feeds milk) over a habitat reason.
Tackle a transfer question: 'Is a shark a mammal?' and give the reason from its features (breathes with gills, does not feed its babies milk → fish).
activities.title: Check and extend: sort, say why, and test a new animal

feedback: Follow the dolphin's answer by connecting it to the child: 'You breathe air too, and you drank milk as a baby — so a dolphin is like you.'
Steer the conversation back to the feature test so the spark leads into sorting or justification.
activities.intendedInsight: The air-breathing proof becomes memorable and personal — the dolphin is 'like us', not like a fish.
learnerActions: Talk in role to a friendly dolphin (or a marine biologist) and ask 'Why do you keep coming up to the top of the water?'
Hear the dolphin explain: 'I have to breathe air like you — that's why I'm not a fish,' and ask a follow-up about how its baby feeds.
activities.title: Optional spark: ask the dolphin why it keeps surfacing
